title: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
summary: The full map of a process, how stack frames and malloc get memory, size-class allocators, the x86-64 page walk, TLB reach, page faults, and what happens when RAM runs out.
outcomes: Read /proc/PID/maps: name each region, its permissions, and how ASLR moves it
Trace how call, ret and rsp create and free stack frames, and estimate how deep recursion can go
Compute the chunk size glibc malloc uses for a request and explain brk versus mmap allocation
Explain how thread caches and size classes make malloc fast, and tell internal from external fragmentation
Split an x86-64 virtual address into page-table indices and offset for 4 KiB and 2 MiB pages
Compute TLB reach and explain when huge pages, PCIDs and TLB shootdowns matter
Explain minor and major page faults, copy-on-write fork and Linux overcommit
Compute average access time under page faults and explain reclaim, swap and thrashing

lessons.title: The map of a process: segments, /proc/PID/maps and ASLR

blocks.md: OSTEP opens its virtual memory chapters with a three-line program that prints the address of `main`, of a `malloc` result and of a local variable. The code address is lowest, the heap comes next, and the stack sits at the far other end of a huge space. Every one of those numbers is a **virtual** address. This lesson draws the whole map of one process on Linux x86-64, so the stack, heap and page-table lessons that follow all have a place to point to.

blocks.caption: Linux only. One variable of each kind, then the process's own map. Build with `cc map.c`, run it twice, and compare.

blocks.md: The map comes from `/proc/PID/maps` (`self` means the reading process). Each line is one **virtual memory area** (VMA): a contiguous range of addresses with one set of permissions and one backing, either a file or nothing. The columns, from [proc_pid_maps(5)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc_pid_maps.5.html) (the number in parentheses is the manual section: 2 for system calls, 3 for library functions, 5 for file formats): the address range; the permissions `r`, `w`, `x`, then `p` for a private mapping (copy-on-write: writes go to a private copy, never back to the file) or `s` for a shared one; the offset into the file; the device and inode (a file's number on its file system; 0 means no file); and the path. A blank path is an **anonymous mapping**, memory backed by no file. Pseudo-paths name the special ones: `[heap]`, `[stack]` and `[vdso]`.

blocks.caption: Real lines from the example in proc_pid_maps(5), from an older program loaded at a fixed address, with some lines left out. Note the lines per file: code r-xp, read-only data r--p, writable data rw-p (the full example also has a ---p gap line inside libc).

blocks.title: One process, low addresses on the left

scenes.caption: Not to scale. The executable's own pieces come first: code (text), read-only constants such as string literals (rodata), initialized globals (data) and zero-initialized globals (bss).

The [heap] starts above bss: right at its end without heap randomization, a random distance above it at the default randomize_va_space = 2. malloc(100) lands here, and the heap grows upward as glibc moves its top edge, the program break.
Far above, in a wide area below the stack: the 1 MiB malloc as an anonymous mapping (blank pathname) and shared libraries such as libc, each mapped from its file.

The [stack] sits near the top of the user half and grows down toward the mappings. rsp, the stack pointer register, marks its top (next lesson). The [vdso] (virtual dynamic shared object) is a small library the kernel maps into every process.
The gaps (...) are most of the space. They have no VMA and no page tables, so they cost nothing, and touching them gets SIGSEGV, the signal for an invalid memory access.
Permissions: no region is both writable and executable. Code and the vdso are r-x, rodata is read-only, and data, heap, mappings and stack are rw-.

blocks.md: Two facts about this picture matter for every later lesson. First, it is **sparse**. On x86-64, Linux gives each process about 128 TiB of user addresses, a number the page-walk lesson derives (MiB, GiB and TiB are binary units of $2^{20}$, $2^{30}$ and $2^{40}$ bytes), and a typical program's VMAs add up to a few megabytes or gigabytes. Second, the kernel keeps this list of VMAs for every process. When a later lesson says a page fault handler checks that an address lies in a valid region, these lines are the regions it checks.

Which way things grow follows from the layout. The heap starts above bss (at a random distance under the default ASLR setting, below) and grows upward as the C library raises the *program break*, the heap's top edge, with the `brk` system call. On Linux that library is usually **glibc**, the GNU C library. The main thread's stack grows downward from near the top, and the kernel keeps a guard gap below it (next lesson). Large `malloc` blocks, thread stacks and shared libraries are placed in the wide area in between, each by the `mmap` system call, which maps a new range of pages into the address space. As OSTEP points out, every process uses memory-mapped files even if it never calls `mmap`, because the loader maps the executable and its shared libraries this way.

**Permissions** are enforced by hardware. Each page-table entry carries them, including the NX (no-execute) bit, which AMD added to x86 and Intel matched with XD: the CPU refuses to run instructions from a page marked no-execute. So bytes an attacker manages to write onto the stack or heap cannot simply be executed. A program changes a range's permissions with `mprotect(2)`. A page with no permissions at all (`PROT_NONE`) is a **guard page**: any access faults, which turns running off the end of a stack into an immediate SIGSEGV instead of silent corruption.

scenes.caption: OSTEP runs a three-line program that prints the address of a local variable. Run 1 on a modern Linux system prints 0x7ffd3e55d2b4.
Run 2 prints 0x7ffe1033b8f4: the stack moved by about 3.3 GiB. Even the low 12 bits changed, so the variable's offset within its page moved too.
Run 3 prints 0x7ffe45522e94, about 4.1 GiB above run 1. Every run gets a new layout.
The kernel picks these offsets itself, under the control of kernel.randomize_va_space. Set it to 0 and the three runs would print the same address.

blocks.md: **Address space layout randomization** (ASLR) is why your two runs print different numbers. The kernel setting `kernel.randomize_va_space` ([sysctl docs](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/sysctl/kernel.html)) has three values: 0 turns it off; 1 randomizes the mmap base, the stack and the vdso, and so shared libraries and the code of position-independent executables (PIE) too; 2 also randomizes the heap and is the default unless the kernel was built with `CONFIG_COMPAT_BRK`. The point, per OSTEP, is defense: attacks that hijack a return address (return-to-libc, return-oriented programming) need to know where useful code sits, and with random placement most such attempts crash instead of taking control.

blocks.prompt: A program computes a pointer that lands in the gap between the heap and the mapping area, and writes to it. The page tables have no entry for it. What does the kernel do?
blocks.reveal: It sends **SIGSEGV**. The MMU raises a page fault, the kernel looks for a VMA containing the address, finds none, and has nothing to fix. Contrast this with a fault inside a VMA that simply has no frame yet: that one the kernel fills in and the program never notices (the page-fault lesson). A fault only becomes a crash when the address is outside every VMA or the access breaks the VMA's permissions.

blocks.md: A big line in `/proc/PID/maps` is not memory in use. A VMA only says which addresses the program may touch; Linux's memory concepts docs note that anonymous mappings usually just define those areas, and physical pages arrive on first access. A 1 GiB mapping that was never written uses almost no RAM.

A process is one sparse virtual address space: a handful of VMAs (code, data, bss, heap, mappings, libraries, stack, vdso), each with its own permissions and backing, separated by vast unmapped gaps, at addresses ASLR moves on every run.

blocks.question: Which line of `/proc/self/maps` contains the global `int counter = 7;` from the program above?
options: The executable's r-xp line
The [heap] line
The executable's rw-p line
The [stack] line
blocks.explain: An initialized global is part of the data segment, loaded from the executable file and writable, so it lives in the executable's rw-p mapping. Code is r-xp and not writable; the heap only holds malloc'ed blocks; the stack holds locals like `local`.

blocks.question: A machine runs with `kernel.randomize_va_space = 1`. Across runs of a PIE program, which region keeps the same position relative to the program's own data segment?
options: The [heap], because heap randomization is only added at setting 2
The [stack]
Shared libraries such as libc
The [vdso]
blocks.explain: Setting 1 randomizes the mmap base, the stack and the vdso (so libraries move too) and the PIE code start; the data segment moves with the code. Only setting 2 adds heap randomization, so at 1 the heap starts right where bss ends, run after run.

lessons.title: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns

blocks.md: Every running function needs scratch space: its arguments, its local variables, and the address to jump back to when it finishes. Function calls nest and unwind in strict last in, first out (LIFO) order: if `main` calls `sum`, `sum` must finish before `main` resumes. A **stack** is the data structure that matches that order exactly, so every process gets one, managed directly by the CPU's call instructions.

On x86-64, register `rsp` (the **stack pointer**) holds the address of the top of the stack, and the stack grows toward **lower** addresses. The `call` instruction pushes the return address (subtract 8 from `rsp`, store), and `ret` pops it back. A function then reserves room for its locals with a single subtraction from `rsp`. That block of memory, from the return address down to the new `rsp`, is the function's **stack frame**. Unoptimized code also saves the caller's `rbp` (the **frame pointer**, a register pointing at the current frame) in a short entry sequence called the **prologue**. The exact frame rules (where arguments go, how the stack must be aligned) are fixed by the platform's **application binary interface** (ABI): the conventions all compiled code on a platform follows, so that functions built separately, even by different compilers, can call each other.

blocks.caption: A tiny recursive function. Unoptimized builds give each call its own frame; with optimization a compiler may turn this recursion into a loop and use no extra frames.

blocks.title: Frames pile up, then unwind

scenes.caption: Simplified model: each sum frame is 32 bytes (return address, saved rbp, the local rest, padding). Before main's call, rsp = 0x7ffe1000, a multiple of 16 as the ABI requires.
call sum(2) pushes the return address, the prologue saves rbp and subtracts 16. The whole frame costs a few instructions, no matter how many locals it holds.
sum(1) gets a fresh frame 32 bytes lower. Each call has its own n and rest, which is why recursion works at all.
sum(0) is the deepest frame. rsp is now 0x60 = 96 bytes below where main started.
sum(0) returns 0. ret pops the return address and rsp moves back up: freeing the frame was just pointer arithmetic, nothing was erased.
sum(1) returns 1 to sum(2), which computes 2 + 1.
Back in main, rsp is 0x7ffe1000 again. All three frames are gone in O(1) each, with no bookkeeping.

blocks.title: The same stack, 8 bytes per cell

scenes.caption: Addresses 0x7ffe0ff8 down to 0x7ffe0fa0, only the low 12 bits shown. Nothing is in use yet; rsp sits at 0x7ffe1000, just above the left edge.
sum(2): return address into main, saved rbp, its local rest and 8 bytes of padding that keep rsp 16-byte aligned.
sum(1) and sum(0) stack their frames below. The stack only ever grows and shrinks at one end.
After two returns rsp is back at 0x7ffe0fe0. The old bytes of the dead frames are still there (muted): the next call simply overwrites them.

blocks.md: Linux uses the System V ABI, named after AT&T's UNIX System V where it began, and its processor-specific supplement for x86-64 is called the **psABI**. Two of its rules shape every frame. First, `rsp` must be 16-byte aligned just before a `call`, so frames are padded to multiples of 16. Second, the 128 bytes just below `rsp`, the **red zone**, are reserved. A **signal** is the kernel's way of interrupting a process to report an event, and unless the process asks otherwise, the handler function it registered for that event runs on the interrupted thread's own stack, below `rsp`. Signal and interrupt handlers must not touch those 128 bytes, so a leaf function (one that calls nothing) may keep its whole frame there without moving `rsp` at all.

blocks.prompt: The default stack size limit on many Linux systems is 8 MiB (`ulimit -s` prints 8192, in kibibytes, KiB, units of 1024 bytes). With 32-byte frames as in our model, roughly how deep can `sum` recurse before the program crashes?
blocks.reveal: About $8 \times 2^{20} / 32 = 262,144$ frames (minus whatever main and the C runtime already use). Then the next push touches memory below the limit and the process gets **SIGSEGV** (from *segmentation violation*), a *stack overflow*. Real frames are often larger than 32 bytes, so the real limit is lower. This is why deep recursion over untrusted input (say, parsing deeply nested JSON) is a classic crash bug.

blocks.md: Where the limits come from on Linux: the main thread's stack grows on demand, up to the `RLIMIT_STACK` resource limit, the per-process cap that `ulimit -s` shows ([getrlimit(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/getrlimit.2.html)). Hitting it raises SIGSEGV. The kernel also keeps a guard gap below the stack where no other mapping may be placed, 256 pages by default (1 MiB with 4 KiB pages). Other threads get a **fixed-size** stack chosen at creation: with glibc it defaults to the `RLIMIT_STACK` soft limit (the value actually enforced, which a process may raise up to a separate hard limit), or 2 MB on most architectures if that limit is unlimited ([pthread_create(3)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_create.3.html)).

blocks.prompt: A worker thread is created with default attributes, so its stack is a fixed 8 MiB (the RLIMIT_STACK soft limit). It calls a function that declares `char buf[16 << 20];` (16 MiB) and writes `buf[0] = 1`. What happens?
blocks.reveal: Reserving the frame cannot fail: it is one `sub` on `rsp`. The write then lands about 16 MiB below the stack top, past the end of the 8 MiB stack and past its guard area, which is one page by default ([pthread_attr_setguardsize(3)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_attr_setguardsize.3.html)). If nothing is mapped there, SIGSEGV. If another mapping sits there, such as another thread's stack, the write silently corrupts it. GCC's `-fstack-clash-protection` allocates large frames one page at a time and touches each page, so the guard is always hit. Big buffers belong on the heap.

blocks.md: Look again at the frame figure: the return address sits at a higher address than the locals. Writing past the end of a local array climbs toward higher addresses, through the saved `rbp` and into the return address, so the function's `ret` jumps wherever the overflowing bytes say. OSTEP's example is a `strcpy` of untrusted input into a 100-byte local buffer. GCC's [`-fstack-protector`](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Instrumentation-Options.html) adds a guard value (a *canary*) to functions with such buffers, sets it on entry and checks it before returning; if it changed, the program prints an error and exits. The NX bit and ASLR from the first lesson are the other two layers of defense.

The stack is not faster *memory*. Stack and heap bytes live in the same RAM behind the same caches. What is cheaper is *allocation*: one `sub` on `rsp` versus a search through allocator data structures. The top of the stack is also almost always hot in cache because it is reused constantly.

Stack memory lives exactly as long as the function call that created it. Allocation and release are a pointer adjustment, which is why the size must be bounded and why anything that must outlive the call has to go somewhere else: the heap.

blocks.question: A function returns `&x`, where `x` is one of its local variables. The caller reads the pointer immediately and gets the right value, but after calling `printf` it reads garbage. Why?
options: The compiler moved x to the heap, and printf freed it
x's frame was released on return; printf's own frame reused those stack bytes
Reading a stack variable from another function always raises SIGSEGV
The red zone is cleared by the kernel on every return
blocks.explain: Returning only moves `rsp` back up; the bytes are not erased, so an immediate read may look fine. The next call (here `printf`) pushes its frame into the same addresses and overwrites them. No fault occurs because the memory is still mapped, which is what makes this bug so sneaky. The red zone is never cleared by the kernel.

blocks.question: Why can a leaf function on x86-64 Linux often skip adjusting `rsp` entirely?
options: Leaf functions run in kernel mode and use the kernel stack
The CPU automatically allocates a frame on every call
Leaf functions cannot have local variables
The 128-byte red zone below rsp is guaranteed not to be clobbered by signal or interrupt handlers
blocks.explain: The psABI reserves 128 bytes below `rsp` that handlers must not modify. A function that calls nothing can keep its locals there, since no callee will push into that space. Saving the `sub`/`add` pair is a small win on very hot leaf functions.

lessons.title: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory

blocks.md: Some data cannot live on the stack: its size is only known at run time, it must outlive the function that created it, or it is too large for a bounded stack. That data goes on the **heap**, a region managed by a user-space library (`malloc` and `free` in C). The library hands out pieces of a big region and takes them back in *any* order, which is exactly what makes it harder than a stack.

Because blocks are freed in arbitrary order, free space ends up scattered. An allocator tracks it in a **free list**, a list of the free chunks with each one's address and length, and relies on two mechanisms (OSTEP chapter 17). **Splitting**: to serve a small request from a bigger free chunk, cut the chunk in two and keep the remainder on the list. **Coalescing**: when a chunk is freed, merge it with free neighbours so large requests can still succeed.

scenes.caption: OSTEP's example heap of 30 bytes, drawn as six 5-byte cells. Bytes 0 to 9 and 20 to 29 are free, 10 to 19 are in use. The free list holds two 10-byte entries.
A request for 15 bytes fails even though 20 bytes are free in total: no single free chunk is big enough. That is external fragmentation.
malloc(1) is served by splitting the chunk at 20: byte 20 is returned, and the free entry becomes address 21, length 9 (cell 20-24 now mixed).
Back to the original heap, now free(10). Without coalescing the list shows three 10-byte chunks and a 20-byte request still fails.
With coalescing the freed chunk merges with both neighbours into a single 30-byte chunk, so any request up to 30 bytes can succeed.

blocks.md: Real allocators also need to know a block's size when you call `free(p)`, which gets no size argument. glibc's malloc stores it in a hidden header word just before the pointer it returns. Each chunk starts with two 8-byte fields: `prev_size`, the size of the chunk before it, and `size`, its own size. `prev_size` is only needed while the previous chunk is free (to merge with it), so while a chunk is in use, the next chunk's `prev_size` slot is lent to it as user data. The net cost of an in-use chunk is just its 8-byte `size` field.

From the comments in glibc's `malloc.c`: on 64-bit systems the alignment is 16 bytes, each in-use chunk carries those 8 bytes of overhead, and the minimum chunk is 32 bytes, so even `malloc(0)` consumes 32 bytes. The rounding rule is the `request2size` macro. It adds the 8-byte header, then adds 15 and clears the low 4 bits with a bitwise AND against the complement of 15. Clearing the low 4 bits rounds down to a multiple of 16, so adding 15 first turns that into rounding up: for `malloc(25)`, 25 + 8 + 15 = 48, which is already a multiple of 16, so the chunk is 48 bytes.

blocks.caption: glibc request2size on 64-bit: add the 8-byte header, round up to a multiple of 16, never below the 32-byte minimum. Usable size is chunk minus 8.

blocks.title: What a small malloc really costs (glibc, 64-bit)

scenes.caption: Bytes requested by the program.

Chunk size glibc carves from the heap, computed with request2size. 24 bytes fit in the 32-byte minimum because the next chunk's prev_size field, unused while your chunk is in use, is lent to you; 25 bytes tips into 48.

Bytes consumed beyond the request: 31 bytes for a 1-byte malloc. Millions of tiny heap objects pay this tax, which is why pools exist: custom allocators that carve many small objects out of one big block, with little or no per-object header.

blocks.md:
Where does the heap get memory from the kernel? glibc uses two routes ([malloc(3)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/malloc.3.html), [mallopt(3)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/mallopt.3.html)):

- **Small requests** come from the main heap, the `[heap]` region that sits above the program's data and bss segments in the first lesson's map, and grows upward by moving its top edge, the *program break*, with the `brk`/`sbrk` system calls. Freed chunks go on free lists for reuse, and the heap can only be trimmed from its top end.
- **Large requests** (at least `M_MMAP_THRESHOLD`, 128 KiB by default) that the free lists cannot satisfy get their own private anonymous `mmap`. The `mmap` system call maps a new range of pages into the address space; *anonymous* means the pages are backed by no file and start out zero-filled. `free` returns them to the kernel immediately (with `munmap`), but each one costs system calls and kernel page zeroing (the kernel must clear every new page so no data leaks from its previous owner).

The threshold is dynamic by default: when a mmap-backed block larger than the current threshold (and at most 32 MiB on 64-bit) is freed, glibc raises the threshold to that size, betting that the program will keep allocating blocks that big. Multithreaded programs add one more layer: to avoid lock contention glibc creates extra **arenas**, separate heaps with their own mutexes, and keeps a small per-thread cache of recently freed chunks. The next lesson shows how those caches and bins work.

`free` rarely shrinks your process. Freed small chunks go back on glibc's free lists, not to the kernel, and a single live chunk near the top of the heap blocks trimming. A process whose memory never drops after a burst is usually not leaking; check whether the memory is reusable before hunting leaks.
Stack: LIFO, bounded, freed by returning, one instruction. Heap: any order, any size, any lifetime, paid for with headers, rounding, free-list searches and fragmentation.

blocks.question: On 64-bit glibc, how many heap bytes does `malloc(25)` consume?
blocks.explain: request2size computes (25 + 8 + 15) rounded down to a multiple of 16 = 48. The 8-byte header pushes 25 bytes past the 32-byte minimum chunk, whose usable size is only 24.

blocks.question: A server allocates and frees many 200 KiB buffers. After the first one is freed, later allocations of the same size stop showing up as mmap calls in strace (a tool that logs every system call a process makes). Why?
options: The dynamic mmap threshold rose to the size of the freed block, so new 200 KiB requests are served from the heap
glibc caches the mmap call result in the kernel
200 KiB is below the default 128 KiB threshold
The kernel merged the mappings into the stack
blocks.explain: Freeing an mmap-backed block larger than the current threshold (but at most the 32 MiB cap on 64-bit) raises the threshold to that size. From then on 200 KiB requests come from the brk heap and its free lists, avoiding mmap, munmap and page zeroing on each cycle.

lessons.title: Beyond the basic chunk: size classes, thread caches and fragmentation

blocks.md: The last lesson's allocator keeps one free list and searches it. Picture a server with 32 threads, each doing millions of `malloc(40)` and `free` per second. A single list means one lock that every thread fights over, and a search through chunks of every size to find one that fits. Real allocators avoid both with two ideas: keep a separate list per size, and give each thread (or each CPU) its own cache so the common case touches no lock at all.

glibc does this in layers, all visible in its `malloc.c` and `arena.c`. Each thread has a **tcache** (thread cache): by default 64 singly linked lists, one per chunk size from 32 to 1,040 bytes in 16-byte steps, so requests up to 1,032 bytes (since 2.42 a tunable can add lists for larger sizes). Behind it each **arena** (a heap with its own mutex; on 64-bit, up to 8 per CPU core through glibc 2.43, and since 2.44 at most the larger of 8 and the core count) keeps bins: an *unsorted* bin where freed chunks wait, *small bins* that each hold one exact size below 1,024 bytes, and *large bins* that each hold a range of sizes. Since glibc 2.43 each tcache list holds at most 16 chunks; older releases held 7 and had one more layer, *fastbins*, which 2.43 removed.

blocks.title: Where glibc looks for a 40-byte chunk

scenes.caption: Simplified from glibc's malloc.c. The fast path: this thread's tcache has a list for 48-byte chunks. If it is non-empty, pop one. No lock, a handful of instructions.
The list is empty, so malloc goes to the thread's arena, a heap with its own mutex. Extra arenas exist so threads rarely wait for the same lock.
Inside the arena: the small bin holding exactly 48-byte chunks; then the unsorted bin of recently freed chunks, each sorted into its bin unless it fits; then larger bins, splitting a bigger chunk.
No free chunk fits, so malloc splits 48 bytes off the top chunk, the free space at the end of the heap. If that is too small, the heap grows with a system call.
free reverses the fast path: the chunk goes into this thread's tcache unless that size's list is full (16 in current glibc), and only then back to the arena, where it can merge with free neighbours.

blocks.prompt: Thread A allocates 40-byte objects and passes them to thread B, which frees them. In glibc, where does each freed chunk go first?
blocks.reveal: Into **thread B's** tcache, since the tcache belongs to the freeing thread, whatever arena the chunk came from. Once B's list for that size is full, further frees go back to the chunk's own arena. Meanwhile A keeps missing its own tcache and taking its arena's lock. Producer and consumer threads are exactly the pattern TCMalloc's *transfer cache* exists for: per its design doc, it lets memory flow quickly from the CPU or thread that frees it to the one that allocates.

blocks.md: Allocators designed around this from the start, TCMalloc (thread-caching malloc, from Google) and jemalloc (FreeBSD's C library allocator since 2005), go further with **size classes**. Every small request is rounded up to one of a fixed set of sizes: TCMalloc's design doc gives 60 to 80 classes and the example that 12 bytes rounds to the 16-byte class. Objects of one class are carved from runs of pages that hold only that class, called **spans** in TCMalloc and **slabs** in jemalloc. Because an object's address tells the allocator which span it is in, and the span records the class, objects need no header at all.

blocks.title: A slab of 48-byte slots and its bitmap

scenes.caption: Simplified slab: one run of memory cut into eight 48-byte slots, plus a bitmap with one bit per slot. No headers: the slab, not the object, records the size.
Three malloc(40) calls are rounded up to the 48-byte class and take slots 0, 1 and 2. Finding a slot means finding a 0 bit.
malloc(33) and malloc(48) round to the same class and take slots 3 and 4. Any request from 33 to 48 bytes lands in this slab.
Free slots 1 and 3. The holes are exactly one slot wide, and every future request of this class fits any of them, so a slab never has unusable holes.
The next malloc(44) takes slot 1 (this sketch takes the first 0 bit). Reuse is immediate and needs no splitting or merging.
The catch: the slab's memory can go back to the page allocator only when every bit is 0. Here three live objects pin all 384 bytes.

blocks.md: The caches stack up in tiers. TCMalloc's front end is a per-CPU cache (or, in its older mode, per-thread) holding free objects of each class, with no locks. On a miss it takes a *batch* of objects from the middle end, a transfer cache plus a central free list per class, each behind a mutex. That in turn takes whole spans from the back end, the page heap, which gets memory from the OS. jemalloc similarly has per-thread caches for classes up to 32 KiB by default, in front of arenas (by default up to four per CPU). Each tier is slower but shared, and batching means the slow tiers are visited rarely.

Worked rounding, from the size-class table in [jemalloc(3)](https://jemalloc.net/jemalloc.3.html) for 64-bit with 4 KiB pages: classes go 8, 16, 32, 48, ..., 128 in steps of 16, then four classes per doubling: 160, 192, 224, 256, then 320, 384, 448, 512, and so on. So 100 bytes uses 112, 200 uses 224, 600 uses 640, 1,500 uses 1,536. The worst case sits just past a class boundary: 129 bytes takes 160, wasting 31 bytes, 19 percent. The manual states the bound: about 20 percent internal fragmentation for all but the smallest classes.

blocks.title: Header plus rounding vs size classes

scenes.caption: Bytes consumed beyond the request by glibc: request2size adds an 8-byte header, rounds up to 16 and never goes below 32. Total 80 bytes over 2,432 requested, 3.3 percent.
jemalloc's size classes (16-byte quantum, 4 KiB pages): no header, but the classes widen with size. Total 120 bytes over 2,432, 4.9 percent.
Neither wins everywhere: tiny objects favour no headers, mid-sized ones favour fine rounding. Size classes buy speed and no external fragmentation inside a slab, at a bounded rounding cost.

blocks.md: Two kinds of waste, now with names. **Internal fragmentation** is space inside a block the program did not ask for: headers and rounding, as in the chart. **External fragmentation** is free space scattered in pieces too small or too far apart to use, as in the 30-byte heap of the last lesson. Size classes nearly remove external fragmentation within a span, but move it up a level: a span returns to the page heap only when *all* its objects are free (TCMalloc's design doc), so one live object pins a whole span.

Below is a complete size-class allocator in miniature: three classes, one `mmap`'d region split into three parts, a bump pointer for never-used slots, and one LIFO free list per class whose links live inside the free slots themselves. Note how `sc_free` needs no size: the address alone says which part, and so which class, owns the slot. That is TCMalloc's pagemap idea in one line of arithmetic.

blocks.caption: sc.c: a segregated free-list allocator with three size classes. Like the real ones, it stores the free-list link inside the freed slot.

test.c: 3,000 requests of 1 to 128 bytes. With classes 32, 64 and 128, internal waste is 26 percent; for the same uniform 1 to 128 byte sizes, jemalloc's nine classes up to 128 would waste about 10 percent. The last line shows LIFO reuse.

blocks.md: This is why a long-running server's resident memory often creeps up and stays up without any leak. After a burst, the freed objects sit in caches and in partly used spans or heaps, each pinned by a few survivors. Two practical levers: glibc's [malloc_trim(3)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/malloc_trim.3.html) releases free memory, since glibc 2.8 from all arenas and from every chunk with whole free pages; and you can try another allocator without recompiling by preloading it with `LD_PRELOAD`, which makes the dynamic loader ([ld.so(8)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ld.so.8.html)) load that library first so its `malloc` and `free` override glibc's.

Thread caches are a memory-for-speed trade. jemalloc's manual says it plainly: caching makes allocation very fast but increases memory use and fragmentation, since some objects stay parked in each thread's cache. TCMalloc moved to per-CPU caches because per-thread caches made footprint grow with the number of threads.

Fast allocators round requests to size classes, serve each class from same-size slabs or spans, and put a lock-free per-thread or per-CPU cache in front. The costs are bounded rounding waste, memory parked in caches, and spans pinned by a few live objects.

blocks.question: Using jemalloc's size classes (..., 112, 128, 160, 192, ...), how many bytes does a 129-byte request occupy?
blocks.explain: Above 128 the classes are spaced 32 apart (four per doubling from 128 to 256), so 129 rounds to 160. The 31 wasted bytes are about 19 percent, near the roughly 20 percent bound the manual gives. 144 would need a 16-byte step there; 256 would be power-of-two rounding.

blocks.question: After a traffic spike, a service using a size-class allocator frees 90 percent of its small objects, yet its resident memory barely drops. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The allocator must be leaking the freed objects
The kernel ignores munmap while the process is busy
Freed objects sit in caches, and most spans still hold a few live objects, so whole spans cannot be returned
Freed memory is zeroed, which keeps it resident
blocks.explain: A span or slab goes back to the page heap only when every object in it is free. Survivors scattered across many spans pin them all, and per-thread or per-CPU caches hold more. That is fragmentation, not a leak: the memory is reusable by the same process. Purging caches, malloc_trim with glibc, or a different allocator can help.

lessons.title: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit

blocks.md: Stack and heap addresses are **virtual**: the prerequisite course showed that a per-process page table maps virtual page numbers to physical frames, and that a multi-level tree keeps that table small. This lesson makes it exact for x86-64 with 4 KiB pages, so you can take any 64-bit pointer and say precisely which table entries the hardware reads.

The numbers come from the page size. A 4 KiB page needs a 12-bit **offset** ($2^{12} = 4096$). Each page-table node is itself one 4 KiB page of 8-byte entries, so it holds 512 entries and is indexed by 9 bits. Four levels of 9 bits plus the 12-bit offset give $4 \times 9 + 12 = 48$ bits of virtual address. Linux names the levels, from the top, page global directory (PGD), page upper directory (PUD), page middle directory (PMD) and page table entry (PTE), the last level. A fifth name, P4D (page level 4 directory), belongs to the extra level used by 5-level paging and is folded away when the hardware uses only four.

blocks.caption: How x86-64 4-level paging slices a virtual address. To get each level's index, shift the address right by 39, 30, 21 or 12 bits and keep the low 9 bits (mod 512). The shifts are 12 offset bits plus 9 bits per level below.

blocks.md: Bits 63 to 48 are not translated; they must all equal bit 47. Addresses that obey this are **canonical**; anything else faults. The whole $2^{48}$-byte space is $2^8 \times 2^{40}$ = 256 TiB. Bit 47 splits it into two halves, and Linux's x86-64 memory map gives user space the lower one, `0` to `0x00007fffffffffff`, about 128 TiB per process. The kernel lives in the upper half.

scenes.caption: A typical user-space heap pointer, 0x00007f3a12345678. Bit 47 is 0 and bits 63 to 48 are all 0, so it is canonical.
Shift the address right by 39 bits and keep the low 9 (mod 512): 254, so entry 254 of the process's top-level table.
Shifts of 30 and 21 bits give 232 and 145, which pick entries in the next two tables.
A shift of 12 bits gives 325, which selects the PTE. The low 12 bits, 0x678 = 1656, pass through untranslated.

blocks.title: The hardware page walk for one TLB miss

scenes.caption: CR3 holds the physical address of this process's top-level table. Switching processes means loading a different CR3.
Each step reads one 8-byte entry from memory to find the next table. Entry 254, then 232, then 145.
PTE 325 holds frame number 0x1a2b3 (a made-up value). Physical address = 0x1a2b3 x 4096 + 0x678 = 0x1a2b3678. Four dependent memory reads before the real access.
Huge page: if the PMD entry has its page-size bit set it maps a 2 MiB frame directly. The walk stops one level early and the low 21 bits, 0x145678, become the offset.

blocks.md: The same trick works one level higher: a PUD entry can map a 1 GiB page, leaving a 30-bit offset. Linux's documentation describes exactly this: on x86, 2M and 1G pages are mapped by entries in the second and third level tables. Each table level also tells you how much memory one full table covers: a PTE table maps $512 \times 4$ KiB = 2 MiB, a PMD table 1 GiB, a PUD table 512 GiB.

Newer CPUs add a fifth level ([5-level paging](https://docs.kernel.org/arch/x86/x86_64/5level-paging.html)): 9 more bits give 57-bit virtual addresses, 128 PiB in total (a pebibyte, PiB, is $2^{50}$ bytes, and $2^{57} = 2^7 \times 2^{50}$ = 128 PiB) and 56 bits for user space. A miss walks one more table. Linux still does not hand out user addresses above 47 bits by default, because some JIT (just-in-time) compilers stash data in the high bits of pointers; a program opts in by passing a high hint address to `mmap`.

A miss does not always cost four DRAM reads. The page-table entries are ordinary data that can sit in the CPU caches, and Linux's page-table docs note that MMUs also keep page walk caches for upper levels. The four loads are the worst case of the structure, not a fixed latency.
Read a pointer as five numbers: four 9-bit table indices and a 12-bit offset. Huge pages simply end the walk early and widen the offset to 21 or 30 bits.

blocks.question: For virtual address 0x00007f3a12345678 mapped with a 2 MiB huge page, which bits form the offset within the page?
options: Bits 11 to 0
Bits 20 to 0
Bits 29 to 0
Bits 47 to 21
blocks.explain: A 2 MiB page is $2^{21}$ bytes, so the offset is the low 21 bits (here 0x145678). The PMD entry maps the page directly, so bits 20 to 12, which would normally index a PTE table, become part of the offset.

blocks.question: A program maps 1 GiB of memory and touches all of it with 4 KiB pages. Roughly how much memory do the last-level page tables alone take?
options: 4 KiB
64 KiB
2 MiB
1 GiB
blocks.explain: 1 GiB / 4 KiB = 262,144 page-table entries at 8 bytes each = 2 MiB, which is 512 PTE tables of 4 KiB. With 2 MiB pages the same gigabyte needs just 512 PMD entries, one 4 KiB table.

lessons.title: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns

blocks.md: A walk of four dependent loads on every access would be ruinous, so the MMU caches finished translations in the **translation lookaside buffer** (TLB). The prerequisite course covered hits and misses. Here the question is quantitative: how much memory can the TLB cover, what happens when your **working set** (the set of pages a program touches within a short window) is bigger, and what flushes it.

**TLB reach** (OSTEP calls it coverage) is the memory a TLB can map at once: number of entries times page size. OSTEP's Culler's Law, named after David Culler, one of the authors' advisors, who kept pointing to the TLB as the source of performance problems, sums up the consequence: RAM isn't always RAM. If a program touches more pages in a short time than the TLB can hold, it takes miss after miss even when the data itself fits in cache. The chart that follows uses a fully associative TLB, meaning any translation can sit in any entry, so only the entry count limits it.

blocks.caption: Model TLB of 1,024 entries. Real CPUs have several TLB levels with separate, model-specific sizes per page size.

blocks.title: Translation overhead vs working set (simple model)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: uniformly random accesses, a fully associative TLB, hit rate = min(1, reach / working set), and a fixed walk cost (30 cycles here is an assumed value, not a measurement).

With 4 KiB pages the overhead appears past 4 MiB: at 64 MiB the hit rate is 4 over 64, one sixteenth, so about 94 percent of accesses miss, and 0.94 times the 30-cycle walk is about 28 extra cycles per access in this model.
2 MiB pages push the knee (the working-set size where the curve bends upward, which is exactly the TLB reach) out 512 times further, to 2 GiB. The same 64 MiB working set now never misses.
Quadrupling the TLB to 4,096 entries moves the 4 KiB knee only to 16 MiB. Huge pages scale reach far more cheaply than bigger TLBs.

blocks.md: Linux offers huge pages two ways ([concepts](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/concepts.html)). **hugetlbfs** (the huge TLB file system, a memory-only file system whose files are backed by huge pages) needs an administrator to reserve huge pages up front and the application to map them explicitly; databases often do this. **Transparent Huge Pages** (THP) needs no code changes: the kernel uses 2 MiB pages for suitable anonymous memory (not backed by a file, like the heap) when it can, and `khugepaged`, a background kernel thread, later collapses runs of small pages into huge ones. THP can be set to `always`, `madvise` (only regions marked with `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)`) or `never`. `madvise` is the system call a program uses to give the kernel advice about how it will use a range of its memory; `MADV_HUGEPAGE` is the advice "please back this range with huge pages".

Huge pages are not free. The THP documentation warns that a process that maps a large region but touches one byte can get a whole 2 MiB page instead of 4 KiB, and allocating a huge page needs 2 MiB of *physically contiguous* memory, which may require compaction: the kernel moves in-use pages around to assemble a free contiguous run. That is why `madvise` mode exists.

The model above is a prediction you can test. Run a random-access loop over a small and a large buffer and count TLB misses with `perf stat`, the Linux profiler's counter mode. perf offers generic event names such as `dTLB-loads` and `dTLB-load-misses` that it maps onto each CPU's own counters; some CPUs lack them, and `perf list` shows what yours has. Then repeat the large run with `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` and check in `/proc/PID/smaps` (the per-region detail behind `/proc/PID/maps`, with memory counters for each VMA) that huge pages were really used: the THP docs say to sum the `AnonHugePages` fields there.

blocks.caption: tlb.c: touch every page of an N MiB buffer, then do 100 million random byte reads. A third argument asks for transparent huge pages.

blocks.code:
cc -O2 tlb.c -o tlb
# 4 MiB fits the model TLB's reach; 512 MiB is far beyond it
perf stat -e dTLB-loads,dTLB-load-misses ./tlb 4
perf stat -e dTLB-loads,dTLB-load-misses ./tlb 512
# same 512 MiB, now with MADV_HUGEPAGE (THP mode must be always or madvise)
perf stat -e dTLB-loads,dTLB-load-misses ./tlb 512 huge
# while a run is in progress: how much of it is backed by huge pages?
awk '/AnonHugePages/ {s += $2} END {print s " kB"}' /proc/$(pgrep -n tlb)/smaps
blocks.caption: What to look for: a large jump in the miss ratio from 4 to 512 MiB, and a sharp drop with huge pages if AnonHugePages is close to 512 MiB. In THP mode always, the plain 512 MiB run may already get huge pages, so check its AnonHugePages too. Exact numbers depend on the CPU's TLB sizes.

blocks.md: The TLB also has to stay correct when mappings change. On a context switch the new process uses different page tables. The simple fix is to flush the whole TLB; OSTEP describes the better one, an **address space identifier** (ASID) tag on each entry. x86 calls it PCID (process-context identifier): with it, Linux can switch page tables without flushing everything ([page table isolation docs](https://docs.kernel.org/arch/x86/pti.html)); without it, every CR3 write flushes the TLB.

Multithreaded programs add a harder case. Threads share one page table, so each CPU running a thread of the process may hold a cached translation. When one thread unmaps memory, the kernel must invalidate that translation everywhere before the memory can be reused. This is a **TLB shootdown**: in Linux's x86 code (`arch/x86/mm/tlb.c`) the initiating CPU sends inter-processor interrupts (IPIs) to the other CPUs using that address space and waits for them to finish flushing. Some newer AMD CPUs can instead broadcast the invalidation in hardware with INVLPGB, a broadcast form of `invlpg`, the instruction that invalidates one page's translation in the local TLB. Current Linux uses it when available.

scenes.caption: A thread unmaps a buffer. CPU 1 is running another thread of the same process and may have the old translation in its TLB.
The kernel clears the page-table entries, then flushes its own TLB entries (one invlpg per page or a full flush, a tradeoff the kernel's x86 TLB docs discuss).
CPU 1 cannot see CPU 0's flush, so CPU 0 interrupts it with an inter-processor interrupt and waits. CPU 1 stops what it was doing to flush.
Only after the acknowledgement may the pages be reused and munmap return. The cost grows with the number of CPUs the process runs on.

blocks.md: TLB reach = entries x page size. Working sets beyond it pay a page walk on most random accesses; huge pages raise reach by 512 times, and every unmap in a multithreaded process may interrupt other CPUs.

blocks.question: A random-access hash table grows from 2 MiB to 512 MiB and slows down more than its cache miss rate explains. Which change most directly targets the extra cost?
options: Use a TLB with twice as many entries
Switch from malloc to calloc
Increase RLIMIT_STACK
Back the table with 2 MiB huge pages (for example madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE))
blocks.explain: 512 MiB of random access is far beyond a 4 KiB-page TLB's reach, so most accesses also need a page walk. 2 MiB pages raise reach 512 times, so the table needs only 256 translations. You cannot buy a bigger TLB in software, and the other options do not touch translation.

blocks.question: Why is calling munmap on a small buffer often slower in a 64-thread process than in a single-threaded one?
options: The kernel must shoot down stale TLB entries on every CPU running the process, using IPIs and waiting for them
munmap must zero the pages first
Each thread has its own page table that must be edited
munmap takes a global lock across all processes
blocks.explain: Threads share one page table, so any CPU running one of them might cache the translation. The initiating CPU interrupts those CPUs and waits for them to flush before the pages can be reused. Threads do not have separate page tables, and freed pages are not zeroed at munmap.

lessons.title: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit

blocks.md: A **page fault** is the exception the MMU raises when a translation fails: the page is not present, or the access breaks its permissions. The prerequisite course treated it as the path to swapping. On modern Linux most faults are something else: the kernel's way of being **lazy**. Linux's page-table docs name the two common, expected causes: lazy allocation and copy-on-write.

When `malloc(64 MiB)` calls `mmap`, the kernel only records a new VMA, one more line in `/proc/PID/maps`; it does not allocate a single physical frame or fill a single PTE. The first touch of each page faults. The handler looks up the VMA containing the address and checks that its permissions allow the access, then allocates a zeroed frame, installs the PTE and returns, and the CPU **retries** the faulting instruction, which now succeeds.

blocks.title: First touch of freshly malloc'ed memory

scenes.caption: malloc of 64 MiB becomes mmap. The kernel records the region and returns an address. No RAM is used yet.
The first store to p[0]: TLB miss, the page walk finds no present PTE, so the MMU raises a page fault.
The address is inside a valid writable region, so this is a minor fault: allocate a zeroed frame, fill the PTE, no disk I/O.
Return from the exception and retry the store, which now hits. The next 4 KiB page will fault again on its first touch.
A store to an address in no valid region (say a dangling pointer into unmapped memory) also faults, but the handler finds nothing to fix and sends SIGSEGV.

blocks.md: `getrusage(2)` counts both kinds of fault per process: `ru_minflt`, faults serviced without I/O, and `ru_majflt`, faults that needed I/O, such as reading a page back from swap or from a memory-mapped file. A minor fault costs a trip into the kernel and zeroing a page; a major fault waits for storage, which is far slower. The final lesson of this course explains swap and memory-mapped files, the two sources of major faults.

blocks.caption: Counting minor faults around a large malloc. Compile with `cc faults.c` on Linux.

blocks.prompt: Run the program above on Linux with 4 KiB pages and THP disabled. Roughly how many faults does the malloc line cause, and how many does the touch loop cause?
blocks.reveal: The malloc line causes very few, about **1 or 2**: mmap only reserves address space, but glibc then writes its chunk header into the first page (and, since this is the program's first malloc, also sets up the thread's tcache on the brk heap). The loop causes about $64\,\text{MiB} / 4\,\text{KiB} = 16,384$ minor faults, one per page on first write (one fewer because malloc already touched the first page, plus a few from the C library itself). With THP set to `always` and a suitably aligned region the kernel can fill 2 MiB per fault, as few as 32 faults, which is the 512x reduction the THP docs describe.

blocks.md: The same laziness makes `fork` cheap. The fork(2) man page says Linux implements it with **copy-on-write** pages: the child gets a copy of the parent's page tables, both pointing at the same frames, marked read-only. Only when either process writes to a page does a fault occur; the kernel then copies that one page and gives the writer a private, writable copy.

scenes.caption: Before fork: the parent's four virtual pages map frames F7, F2, F9 and F4 (made-up frame numbers).
After fork: the child's page table points at the very same frames and both sides are marked read-only. No data was copied.
The child writes to page 1: write to a read-only page, fault. The kernel copies F2 into a new frame F11 and maps it writable for the child only. The parent's F2 stays read-only for now.
If the child now calls exec, its old mappings, F11 included, are dropped. Only one 4 KiB page was ever copied, and the parent's next write to each page just makes it writable again, without copying.

blocks.md: Laziness has a consequence: the kernel hands out more address space than it has RAM, known as **overcommit**. Linux's overcommit accounting has three modes set by `vm.overcommit_memory`: 0 (the default) refuses only obvious overcommits (in the kernel's [mm/util.c](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/mm/util.c), a single request larger than total RAM plus swap); 1 always overcommits; 2 never does, capping total commitments at swap plus a ratio of RAM (50 percent by default). In modes 0 and 1, if pages actually get touched and memory runs out, the **OOM killer** (out of memory) terminates processes to recover. The final lesson covers what the kernel tries before that.

A non-NULL return from `malloc` does not mean the memory exists. Under default overcommit a large allocation succeeds immediately, and the failure, if any, comes later as an OOM kill when the pages are first written, far from the line that allocated them.

Most page faults are normal: they are how Linux allocates memory on first touch and copies pages only on write. Count them with getrusage or `perf stat -e page-faults,major-faults`; worry about major faults and fault storms, not their existence.

blocks.question: A 10 GiB Redis-like process (an in-memory key-value database) calls fork to write a snapshot while it keeps serving writes. Memory use climbs sharply during the snapshot. Why?
options: fork copies all 10 GiB up front
The child process leaks heap memory
Every page the parent writes while the child holds the old version triggers a copy-on-write fault and a new private copy
Copy-on-write is disabled for anonymous memory
blocks.explain: fork only duplicates page tables. But each page the parent modifies during the snapshot must be copied so the child still sees the old data, so memory grows with the number of distinct pages written. Huge pages make this worse: one small write can copy 2 MiB.

blocks.question: A machine has 16 GiB of RAM, no swap and `vm.overcommit_memory = 0`. Processes A and B each malloc 12 GiB and each writes only its first 1 GiB. What most likely happens?
options: B's malloc returns NULL because 24 GiB exceeds RAM
Both mallocs succeed and both run normally: only touched pages use RAM
Both succeed, then the OOM killer immediately kills one of them
The kernel zeroes 24 GiB at malloc time and the machine swaps
blocks.explain: The default heuristic only rejects a single request bigger than RAM plus swap; 12 GiB is not, and it does not add up other processes' reservations. Frames are allocated on first touch, so about 2 GiB of RAM is used. Only if A and B actually wrote more than RAM holds would the OOM killer step in.

lessons.title: When RAM runs out: page cache, file mappings, swap and thrashing

blocks.md: Every frame of RAM holds one of two kinds of page. **Anonymous** pages back the heap, stacks and anonymous `mmap`s; they hold data that exists nowhere else. **File-backed** pages hold a copy of part of a file: the executable and libraries in the first lesson's map, files a program reads, files it maps. The difference decides what the kernel can do when RAM runs short: a clean file page can be dropped and read again later, but an anonymous page must first be written somewhere, to **swap** space on disk.

File pages live in the **page cache**. Linux's memory concepts docs: whenever a file is read, the data goes into the page cache to avoid disk access next time, and writes land there too, marked *dirty* until written back. OSTEP stresses that Linux's page cache is unified: pages reached with `read()` and pages reached through `mmap` are the same frames. Mapping a file ([mmap(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mmap.2.html)) comes in two flavours. `MAP_SHARED` stores go to the cached page and so reach the file. `MAP_PRIVATE` is copy-on-write: stores go to a private copy and never reach the file.

blocks.title: read() and mmap share one page cache

nodes.label:
Process B
mmap of the file

scenes.caption: A reads page 7 of a file. It is not in memory, so the kernel reads it from disk into the page cache, then copies it into A's buffer.
B maps the file and touches page 7: a page fault. The page is already cached, so this is a minor fault: the kernel just points B's PTE at the cached frame. No disk I/O.
Had nobody read page 7 before, B's fault would wait for the disk: a major fault. Same instruction, very different cost, depending only on what is cached.
With MAP_SHARED, B's store goes into the cached page itself. The page is now dirty, A's next read sees the change, and the kernel writes it back to the file later.
With MAP_PRIVATE, B's first store is a copy-on-write fault, as after fork: B gets its own copy of the page, and the file and page cache stay unchanged.

blocks.caption: filemap.c: map a file read-only and read one byte from every 4 KiB page, counting the minor and major faults that causes.

blocks.prompt: Run `filemap` on a 1 GiB file twice: first right after `sync; echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches` (as root; it drops clean page-cache pages), then again. What changes between the runs?
blocks.reveal: Cold run: the pages must come from disk, so you see **major** faults. Expect far fewer than the 262,144 pages, because the kernel reads ahead: madvise(2) describes read-ahead for mapped files, and one disk read brings in many neighbouring pages. Warm run: the whole file is still in the page cache, so there are no major faults and the run is much faster. Minor faults are far fewer than one per page too: on each fault Linux also maps the cached neighbours (*fault-around*, 64 KiB, 16 pages, by default), so expect about 16,384. The program did not change; only the cache did.

blocks.md: When free memory runs low, the kernel **reclaims** pages ([concepts](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/concepts.html)). Below a *low watermark*, the background thread `kswapd` wakes up and frees pages; below the lower *min watermark*, the allocating process itself must reclaim before its allocation can succeed (*direct reclaim*), so it stalls. Clean file pages are cheapest: just drop them. Dirty file pages must be written back first. Anonymous pages can only be swapped out; with no swap configured, they cannot be reclaimed at all, which leaves file pages and, at the end, the OOM killer.

Which page to evict? The ideal is the least recently used one (LRU), but tracking exact recency on every access is far too costly. OSTEP's chapter on replacement policies shows the classic approximation, the **clock algorithm**: frames sit in a circle, and the *use bit* (the hardware-set reference bit from the prerequisite course) tells whether a page was touched since the hand last passed.

blocks.title: The clock algorithm picks a victim

scenes.caption: Eight frames, all full. The hardware sets a page's use (reference) bit on every access. A fault for page I needs a frame; the clock hand points at frame 0.
A's bit is 1: used recently. Clear it, giving A a second chance, and advance.
B's bit is 1 too: clear it and advance.
C's bit is 0: not used since the hand last passed. Evict C and load I into frame 2 with its bit set. The hand moves on to frame 3.
The program touches A again, so the hardware sets A's bit. A has earned another trip around the clock.
A fault for J: D's bit is 1, cleared; E's is 0, so E goes. If E is dirty it must be written out first, which is why kernels prefer clean victims.

blocks.md: Linux's classic version, per OSTEP, is a modified *2Q* (named for its two queues): an **inactive list** for pages accessed once and an **active list** for pages referenced again. Eviction takes from the inactive list, so one big sequential read of a file cannot flush everyone's hot pages out of memory. `/proc/meminfo` shows the sizes as `Active(file)`, `Inactive(file)`, `Active(anon)` and `Inactive(anon)`. Newer kernels can instead use the [multi-gen LRU](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/multigen_lru.html), which keeps several generations of pages rather than two lists.
How bad is a miss? OSTEP computes the **average memory access time** (AMAT): every access pays the memory cost $T_M$, and a fraction $P_{miss}$ also pays the disk cost $T_D$.

blocks.caption: OSTEP's worked numbers: 100 ns memory, 10 ms disk, a 0.1 percent miss rate. The disk term is 100 times the memory term.

blocks.title: Average access time vs page-fault rate

x.label: fraction of accesses that miss RAM

scenes.caption: OSTEP's numbers: 100 ns per memory access, 10 ms per disk access. One miss in a thousand gives 10.1 microseconds on average, about 100 times slower than RAM.
The vertical line is where misses already double the average: one miss in 100,000 accesses. Disk is so slow that a tiny miss rate dominates.
Try a faster device: at an assumed 0.1 ms, the 2x point only moves to one miss in 1,000. Faster storage helps, but each miss still costs as much as 1,000 memory accesses.

blocks.md: Now let the **working set** (the pages a program actively uses) outgrow RAM. Every eviction throws out a page that will be needed again soon, so the miss rate climbs and, by the formula, the machine runs at disk speed. OSTEP calls this **thrashing**: the system spends its time paging instead of computing. Older systems used *admission control*, running fewer processes so the rest fit; Linux, as OSTEP notes, may instead run the OOM killer.

blocks.code:
# per mapping: virtual size, resident, proportional share, swapped
grep -E '^(Size|Rss|Pss|Swap):' /proc/1234/smaps
# system-wide swap-in (si) and swap-out (so) per second, every second
vmstat 1
# page cache size and the active/inactive lists
grep -E '^(Cached|Active|Inactive)' /proc/meminfo
blocks.caption: Commands for spotting memory pressure on Linux (1234 stands for a process ID). Per-process major fault counts come from getrusage, as in the page-fault lesson.

blocks.md: Three sizes, three meanings ([proc_pid_smaps(5)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc_pid_smaps.5.html)). `Size` is the VMA's virtual size, a promise. `Rss` (resident set size) is the part currently in RAM, counting shared pages in full. `Pss` (proportional set size) divides each shared page by the number of processes sharing it; the kernel's proc docs give the example of 1,000 private pages plus 1,000 shared with one other process, a PSS of 1,500. Summing PSS over all processes does not double-count shared libraries; summing RSS does.

Little free memory is not a problem by itself. The page cache deliberately fills idle RAM with file data, and clean cached pages are reclaimable at any moment. Trouble shows up as rates: sustained swap-in and swap-out in `vmstat`, major faults per second, and processes stalled in direct reclaim.

Clean file pages are cheap to evict, dirty ones need write-back, and anonymous ones need swap. The kernel approximates LRU with reference bits and active/inactive lists, but once the working set exceeds RAM, even a 0.1 percent miss rate makes memory 100 times slower: thrashing.

blocks.question: A process maps a 2 GiB file with `MAP_PRIVATE`, writes to 10 of its pages, and exits. What happened to the file on disk?
options: The 10 modified pages were written back at exit
Nothing: private mappings are copy-on-write, so the stores went to private copies
The whole file was rewritten
The write faulted with SIGSEGV because file mappings are read-only
blocks.explain: MAP_PRIVATE creates a private copy-on-write mapping: the first store to each page copies it, and updates are not carried through to the file. Only MAP_SHARED stores reach the page cache page and, through write-back, the file.

blocks.question: A box with no swap is under memory pressure. Which pages can the kernel reclaim?
options: Anonymous heap pages, by zeroing them
Only kernel data structures
Nothing until the OOM killer runs
Clean file pages by dropping them, and dirty file pages after writing them back
blocks.explain: File pages have a home on disk, so they can always be dropped (after write-back if dirty) and re-read later. Anonymous pages have no home except swap; with no swap they stay put, and if file pages are not enough the OOM killer is the last resort.

blocks.question: With $T_M$ = 100 ns and $T_D$ = 10 ms, roughly what average access time does a 1 percent page-fault rate give?
options: About 100 microseconds, 1,000 times slower than RAM
About 1 microsecond
About 10 milliseconds
About 200 nanoseconds
blocks.explain: AMAT = 100 ns + 0.01 x 10 ms = 100 ns + 100 microseconds, about 100.1 microseconds, roughly 1,000 times the 100 ns memory cost. Ten times the miss rate of OSTEP's 0.1 percent example gives ten times the slowdown.
